newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala firing squad executes rapist - murderers.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala firing squad executes rapist - murderers.

text.p: Guatemala's first official firing squad since 1983 executed two child rapists and murderers at dawn on Friday.

Pedro Castillo Mendoza and Roberto Giron died at 8:06 a.m. EDT (1206 GMT) with one pistol shot to the head of each after a forensic doctor determined that a volley of shots from the 16-man firing squad had failed to kill them.
Tied up with green plastic string to small tree trunks against a wall of dirt, the two men met their end without apparent protest.
About 100 photographers and reporters attended the execution, which took place outside the Canada Penal Farm about 36 miles (60 km) south of Guatemala City.

"The blood of Christ," a limp and dazed Castillo mumbled as he was led before two rows of rifle-bearing prison guards. Castillo had a long criminal history, including a conviction for killing his brother 24 years ago.
Giron, a seasonal sugar cane worker with a history of alcoholism, dressed in white clothes and a white cap to face the firing squad.
The execution judge, wearing a black hat, read their sentences. Then a single volley of shots rang out. One of the condemned men slumped, the other's head lolled. There was total silence.
A doctor went up to them, pulled down their lower eyelids and ordered the commander of the firing squad to shoot them both in the side of the head.
As the bodies were loaded into coffins, the execution judge pulled out a pack of menthol cigarettes and lit up.
The execution was scheduled and rescheduled three times while courts ruled on last-minute appeals from the two men, convicted of the 1993 rape and murder of 4-year-old Sonia Marisol Alvarez.

"Every admissible appeal has been used up. There is no more legitimate protection (for the men)," execution judge Gustavo Gaitan Lara told a news conference outside the prison half an hour before the executions.

Gaitan said the appeals, last-minute suspensions, and criticism of the process had been hard, but he added that the execution "shows that our institutions do function despite the fact that there could have been some errors."

A judge originally intended to bar cameras and recorders from the execution but relented at the last minute after reporters threatened to hold them up again while they sought a court order allowing cameras.
